result.summary: Pausanias traces the reign of the Spartan king Cleomenes: his massacre of Argives, his meddling in Athens and Ægina, his bribing of the Delphic priestess to depose Demaratus, and his mad death. The kingdom then passes to Leonidas, whose stand at Thermopylæ and the regent Pausanias' honourable conduct after Platæa are praised.

scenes.title: Cleomenes burns the Argives
scenes.summary: Dorieus leaves to found a colony. Cleomenes defeats the Argives and has the Helots burn the grove where 5,000 fled.
scenes.stakes: The Argives face slaughter in the sacred grove; Cleomenes risks divine anger for burning a sanctuary.

scenes.title: Cleomenes and Athens
scenes.summary: Cleomenes frees Athens from the Pisistratids, then backs Isagoras and ravages Athenian land, including Orgas.
scenes.stakes: The Athenians risk losing their freedom to Isagoras' rule; Cleomenes risks the gods' anger.

scenes.title: Ægina, Demaratus and madness
scenes.summary: Cleomenes arrests Æginetan leaders, then bribes the Delphic priestess to depose Demaratus. He later dies in madness, and each people blames a different offence.
scenes.stakes: Demaratus loses his throne unjustly; Cleomenes faces ruin and divine punishment.

scenes.title: Divine vengeance compared
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives other examples of heroes and gods punishing wrongs and notes that only Cleomenes tampered with the oracle.

scenes.title: Leonidas at Thermopylæ
scenes.summary: Leonidas inherits the kingdom and with 300 Spartans holds Thermopylæ against Xerxes until a Trachinian betrays the pass.
scenes.stakes: Leonidas and his men face death while defending Greece from Persian invasion.

scenes.title: Pausanias after Platæa
scenes.summary: Pausanias, regent for Plistarchus, wins at Platæa, returns a Coan woman home and refuses to outrage Mardonius' body.
scenes.stakes: The Coan woman risks remaining a captive concubine; Mardonius' body risks mutilation.

alias_notes.explanation: Pausanias uses Medes and Persians interchangeably for the Persian empire.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias ranks Leonidas' heroism above all earlier great deeds.
Claims Cleomenes alone dared tamper with the Delphic oracle.

analysis.text: Impiety and abuse of the sacred bring divine punishment, shown by Cleomenes' mad death, while honourable conduct such as Pausanias' is admired.
The chapter condenses Herodotus' account of Spartan kingship and the Persian Wars, showing how Spartan politics and Delphi's authority were intertwined.

legacy.text: Leonidas' stand at Thermopylæ inspired the comic 300 (1998) and the film 300 (2006).

fun_facts.text: Pausanias' account of Cleomenes' death largely follows Herodotus, who also reports that the Spartans blamed it on his bribing the Pythia.

language_notes.text: "A touch of the mad" means Cleomenes was prone to fits of madness, anticipating his later end.
Giving earth and water was the Persian demand for submission; offering them meant acknowledging the Great King's overlordship.
"Caught at some words" means seized upon an old remark: Aristo had publicly doubted that Demaratus was his son.
Protesilaus, the first Greek to die at Troy, had a shrine at Eleus. Artayctes, a Persian governor, plundered it and was punished.
The Trachinian is Ephialtes, who showed the Persians the mountain path round Thermopylæ; the text leaves him unnamed.

context_notes.text: Cleomenes I was a Spartan king of the Agiad house, reigning in the late sixth and early fifth century BC.
Helots were the enslaved population of Laconia and Messenia who worked the land for the Spartans.
Pisistratus' sons Hippias and Hipparchus ruled Athens as tyrants; Sparta helped expel Hippias in 510 BC.
Orgas was a sacred tract near Eleusis, home of the Eleusinian Mysteries of Demeter and Persephone.
Sparta had two kings at once, from the Agiad and Eurypontid families. Demaratus was the Eurypontid.
At Thermopylæ in 480 BC a small Greek force held the narrow pass against Xerxes' huge Persian army.
Pausanias commanded the Greeks at Platæa in 479 BC and later led the fleet to the Hellespont.

literary_notes.text: The casual remark about madness, joined to a horrific act, defines Cleomenes as cruel and unstable.
This gruesome death fulfils the earlier hints of madness and prepares the discussion of divine punishment.
Each people blames the offence that wronged it, showing how every group reads the death as its own vindication.
Pausanias elevates Leonidas above all earlier heroes, a sweeping judgment that expresses his admiration.
The long sentence builds a counterfactual, imagining Xerxes halted, and then closes bluntly with the betrayal and the barbarians crossing over Leonidas' body.
